record.paper_title: Open Problems in Universal Induction & Intelligence
record.original_question: How should the symmetry principle for assigning priors be extended from finite hypothesis classes, where all hypotheses can be taken equally likely, to infinite classes, especially non-compact parameter spaces such as the natural numbers or the real numbers, where classical statistical principles lead to improper distributions that are often unacceptable?

evidence.quote: d) Reparametrization invariance [KW96]. The question is how to extend the symmetry principle from finite hypothesis classes (all hypotheses are equally likely) to infinite hypothesis classes. For “compact” classes, Jeffrey’s prior [Jef46] is a solution, but for non-compact spaces like IN or IR, classical statistical principles lead to improper distributions, which are often not acceptable.

artifact.status_search_result: The question of a universally applicable, reparametrization-invariant proper prior on non-compact parameter spaces (extending the finite-uniform and Jeffreys principles) remains a long-standing open problem in objective Bayesian statistics and universal induction. Universal/Solomonoff-style priors (e.g. 2^{-K(n)} on ℕ) give one ad hoc proper choice, but no canonical rule satisfying all the stated invariance and propriety requirements has been established. No publication identified that resolves this problem.

status_evidence.title: Open Problems in Universal Induction & Intelligence (problem listing)
status_evidence.snippet: Lists reparametrization invariance and the extension of the symmetry principle to non-compact infinite hypothesis classes as an open problem.
status_evidence.claim: The problem of extending the symmetry principle to non-compact parameter spaces is stated as open.

status_evidence.title: Objective Bayesian inference and reference priors (overview)
status_evidence.snippet: Jeffreys' prior is reparametrization invariant but is often improper on non-compact parameter spaces such as ℝ or ℕ.
status_evidence.claim: Standard invariant priors (Jeffreys, reference) are typically improper on non-compact spaces, supporting that the open problem persists.
